claim: Human SESN2 expression is elevated in the colon of ulcerative colitis patients.
source: In this study, we show that human SESN2 expression is elevated in the colon of ulcerative colitis patients but is lost upon p53 inactivation during colon carcinogenesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from patient samples shown in Figure 1B, where SESN2 mRNA expression was analyzed through quantitative RT-PCR of non-inflamed and inflamed colon tissues from UC patients.

claim: Human SESN2 expression is lost upon p53 inactivation during colon carcinogenesis.
source: In this study, we show that human SESN2 expression is elevated in the colon of ulcerative colitis patients but is lost upon p53 inactivation during colon carcinogenesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by data mining of TCGA dataset showing correlation between p53 mutation status and SESN2 expression levels in colon cancer tissues (Figures 3-4).

claim: Sestrin2 is critical for limiting ER stress in mouse colon after inflammatory injury.
source: In mouse colon, Sestrin2 was critical for limiting ER stress and promoting the recovery of epithelial cells after inflammatory injury.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing elevated ER stress markers (BiP, CHOP, p-PERK, XBP1s) in Sesn2-/- mice compared to WT mice after DSS treatment (Figure 2E-H).

claim: Sestrin2 promotes recovery of epithelial cells after inflammatory injury in mouse colon.
source: In mouse colon, Sestrin2 was critical for limiting ER stress and promoting the recovery of epithelial cells after inflammatory injury.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that Sesn2-/- mice failed to recover from DSS-induced colitis, with continued weight loss, decreased colon length, and epithelial degeneration (Figure 1D-F).

claim: Sestrin2 is an important mediator of p53's control over mTORC1 signaling during colitis-promoted tumorigenesis.
source: During colitis-promoted tumorigenesis, Sestrin2 was shown to be an important mediator of p53's control over mTORC1 signaling and tumor cell growth.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing that SESN2 expression correlates with p53 status in human colon cancer (Figure 4), and that Sesn2-/- mice exhibit hyperactive mTORC1 signaling in colon tumors (Figure 6E-L).

claim: Sestrin2 is an important mediator of p53's control over tumor cell growth during colitis-promoted tumorigenesis.
source: During colitis-promoted tumorigenesis, Sestrin2 was shown to be an important mediator of p53's control over mTORC1 signaling and tumor cell growth.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that Sesn2-/- mice develop larger tumors with increased proliferation in the AOM-DSS model (Figure 5C-L).

claim: Sestrin2 downregulation can accelerate colitis.
source: These results highlight Sestrin2 as a novel tumor suppressor, whose downregulation can accelerate both colitis and colon carcinogenesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that Sesn2-/- mice exhibit exacerbated DSS-induced colitis with impaired recovery, increased inflammation markers, and epithelial degeneration (Figures 1-2).

claim: Sestrin2 downregulation can accelerate colon carcinogenesis.
source: These results highlight Sestrin2 as a novel tumor suppressor, whose downregulation can accelerate both colitis and colon carcinogenesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that Sesn2-/- mice develop larger tumors with increased tumor burden in the AOM-DSS model (Figure 5).

claim: Sestrin2 functions as a novel tumor suppressor.
source: These results highlight Sestrin2 as a novel tumor suppressor, whose downregulation can accelerate both colitis and colon carcinogenesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple lines of evidence: SESN2 is downregulated in human colon cancer (Figure 3), Sesn2 loss promotes tumor growth in mice (Figure 5), and Sestrin2 inhibits mTORC1 signaling and cancer cell proliferation (Figures 6-7).

claim: The lifetime risk of developing CRC in the US is 4–5%.
source: The lifetime risk of developing CRC in the US is 4–5%, and approximately one-third of CRC patients die from the disease (Siegel et al, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Siegel et al, 2015.

claim: Approximately one-third of CRC patients die from the disease.
source: The lifetime risk of developing CRC in the US is 4–5%, and approximately one-third of CRC patients die from the disease (Siegel et al, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Siegel et al, 2015.

claim: mTORC1 plays a key tumorigenic role during CRC development induced by colitis.
source: In addition to these components, mammalian target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1), a protein kinase that is essential for cell growth (Hay and Sonenberg, 2004; Zoncu et al, 2011), was recently found to play a key tumorigenic role during CRC development induced by either colitis (Thiem et al, 2013) or a genetic mutation (Faller et al, 2015; Hardiman et al, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Thiem et al, 2013.

claim: mTORC1 plays a key tumorigenic role during CRC development induced by genetic mutation.
source: In addition to these components, mammalian target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1), a protein kinase that is essential for cell growth (Hay and Sonenberg, 2004; Zoncu et al, 2011), was recently found to play a key tumorigenic role during CRC development induced by either colitis (Thiem et al, 2013) or a genetic mutation (Faller et al, 2015; Hardiman et al, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Faller et al, 2015 and Hardiman et al, 2014.

claim: mTORC1 hyperactivation can lead to unrestricted protein synthesis.
source: In addition to promoting cancer cell growth, mTORC1 hyperactivation can lead to unrestricted protein synthesis, resulting in the accumulation of unfolded protein, endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress and tissue injury (Ozcan et al, 2008; Park et al, 2014; Young et al, 2013), which together can contribute to tumor progression (Wang and Kaufman, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ozcan et al, 2008; Park et al, 2014; Young et al, 2013.

claim: mTORC1 hyperactivation results in the accumulation of unfolded protein.
source: In addition to promoting cancer cell growth, mTORC1 hyperactivation can lead to unrestricted protein synthesis, resulting in the accumulation of unfolded protein, endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress and tissue injury (Ozcan et al, 2008; Park et al, 2014; Young et al, 2013), which together can contribute to tumor progression (Wang and Kaufman, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ozcan et al, 2008; Park et al, 2014; Young et al, 2013.

claim: mTORC1 hyperactivation results in endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress.
source: In addition to promoting cancer cell growth, mTORC1 hyperactivation can lead to unrestricted protein synthesis, resulting in the accumulation of unfolded protein, endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress and tissue injury (Ozcan et al, 2008; Park et al, 2014; Young et al, 2013), which together can contribute to tumor progression (Wang and Kaufman, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ozcan et al, 2008; Park et al, 2014; Young et al, 2013.

claim: mTORC1 hyperactivation results in tissue injury.
source: In addition to promoting cancer cell growth, mTORC1 hyperactivation can lead to unrestricted protein synthesis, resulting in the accumulation of unfolded protein, endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress and tissue injury (Ozcan et al, 2008; Park et al, 2014; Young et al, 2013), which together can contribute to tumor progression (Wang and Kaufman, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ozcan et al, 2008; Park et al, 2014; Young et al, 2013.

claim: ER stress is critically involved in the pathogenesis of colitis and colon inflammation.
source: ER stress has been shown to be critically involved in the pathogenesis of colitis and colon inflammation (Bertolotti et al, 2001; Cao et al, 2013; Kaser et al, 2008), which is an important risk factor of CRC development (Thorsteinsdottir et al, 2011) and a well-characterized tumor promoter (Grivennikov et al, 2012; Terzic et al, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bertolotti et al, 2001; Cao et al, 2013; Kaser et al, 2008.

claim: Colon inflammation is an important risk factor of CRC development.
source: ER stress has been shown to be critically involved in the pathogenesis of colitis and colon inflammation (Bertolotti et al, 2001; Cao et al, 2013; Kaser et al, 2008), which is an important risk factor of CRC development (Thorsteinsdottir et al, 2011) and a well-characterized tumor promoter (Grivennikov et al, 2012; Terzic et al, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Thorsteinsdottir et al, 2011.

claim: Colon inflammation is a well-characterized tumor promoter.
source: ER stress has been shown to be critically involved in the pathogenesis of colitis and colon inflammation (Bertolotti et al, 2001; Cao et al, 2013; Kaser et al, 2008), which is an important risk factor of CRC development (Thorsteinsdottir et al, 2011) and a well-characterized tumor promoter (Grivennikov et al, 2012; Terzic et al, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Grivennikov et al, 2012; Terzic et al, 2010.

claim: Sestrins are a family of stress-inducible proteins that are widely conserved throughout animal species.
source: Sestrins are a family of stress-inducible proteins that are widely conserved throughout animal species (Lee et al, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lee et al, 2013.

claim: Sestrins were originally identified as a target of the tumor suppressor p53.
source: Sestrins were originally identified as a target of the tumor suppressor p53 (Budanov et al, 2002; Velasco-Miguel et al, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Budanov et al, 2002; Velasco-Miguel et al, 1999.

claim: Sestrins suppress reactive oxygen species (ROS).
source: Sestrins have two important functions, suppressing reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Budanov et al, 2004) and inhibiting mTORC1 (Budanov and Karin, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Budanov et al, 2004.

claim: Sestrins inhibit mTORC1.
source: Sestrins have two important functions, suppressing reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Budanov et al, 2004) and inhibiting mTORC1 (Budanov and Karin, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Budanov and Karin, 2008.

claim: The ROS-suppressing effect of Sestrins is dependent, at least partially, on mTORC1 inhibition.
source: The ROS-suppressing effect of Sestrins is dependent, at least partially, on mTORC1 inhibition, which promotes autophagic degradation of dysfunctional mitochondria or an Nrf2 inhibitor Keap1 (Bae et al, 2013; Lee et al, 2010; Woo et al, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bae et al, 2013; Lee et al, 2010; Woo et al, 2009.

claim: Sestrin can function as an active oxidoreductase that can directly detoxify ROS such as alkylhydroperoxides.
source: However, Sestrin can also function as an active oxidoreductase that can directly detoxify ROS such as alkylhydroperoxides (Kim et al, 2015a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kim et al, 2015a.

claim: Sestrins inhibit mTORC1 through the activation of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) and the subsequent inactivation of Rheb GTPases.
source: Sestrins inhibit mTORC1 through the activation of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) and the subsequent inactivation of Rheb GTPases (Budanov and Karin, 2008; Sanli et al, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Budanov and Karin, 2008; Sanli et al, 2012.

claim: Sestrins can inhibit Rag GTPases independently of AMPK.
source: Independently of AMPK, Sestrins can also inhibit Rag GTPases (Chantranupong et al, 2014; Kim et al, 2015b; Parmigiani et al, 2014; Peng et al, 2014), which are essential for mTORC1 activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chantranupong et al, 2014; Kim et al, 2015b; Parmigiani et al, 2014; Peng et al, 2014.

claim: Rag GTPases are essential for mTORC1 activity.
source: Independently of AMPK, Sestrins can also inhibit Rag GTPases (Chantranupong et al, 2014; Kim et al, 2015b; Parmigiani et al, 2014; Peng et al, 2014), which are essential for mTORC1 activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chantranupong et al, 2014; Kim et al, 2015b; Parmigiani et al, 2014; Peng et al, 2014.

claim: Sestrin-mediated inhibition of mTORC1 is critical for limiting protein synthesis upon unfolded protein accumulation.
source: Sestrin-mediated inhibition of mTORC1 is also critical for limiting protein synthesis upon unfolded protein accumulation (Bruning et al, 2013; Park et al, 2014) or amino acid starvation (Peng et al, 2014; Wolfson et al, 2015; Ye et al, 2015), thereby suppressing ER stress or nutrient crisis.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bruning et al, 2013; Park et al, 2014.

claim: Sestrin-mediated inhibition of mTORC1 is critical for limiting protein synthesis upon amino acid starvation.
source: Sestrin-mediated inhibition of mTORC1 is also critical for limiting protein synthesis upon unfolded protein accumulation (Bruning et al, 2013; Park et al, 2014) or amino acid starvation (Peng et al, 2014; Wolfson et al, 2015; Ye et al, 2015), thereby suppressing ER stress or nutrient crisis.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Peng et al, 2014; Wolfson et al, 2015; Ye et al, 2015.

claim: SESN1 mRNA was unaltered in ulcerative colitis.
source: Sestrin1 mRNA (SESN1) was unaltered in UC (Figure 1A); however, expression of SESN2 (Figure 1B) and SESN3 (Figure 1C) was significantly increased in the intestine of patients with UC.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative RT-PCR data from UC patient samples shown in Figure 1A.

claim: SESN2 expression was significantly increased in the intestine of patients with ulcerative colitis.
source: Sestrin1 mRNA (SESN1) was unaltered in UC (Figure 1A); however, expression of SESN2 (Figure 1B) and SESN3 (Figure 1C) was significantly increased in the intestine of patients with UC.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative RT-PCR data from UC patient samples shown in Figure 1B.

claim: SESN3 expression was significantly increased in the intestine of patients with ulcerative colitis.
source: Sestrin1 mRNA (SESN1) was unaltered in UC (Figure 1A); however, expression of SESN2 (Figure 1B) and SESN3 (Figure 1C) was significantly increased in the intestine of patients with UC.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative RT-PCR data from UC patient samples shown in Figure 1C.

claim: DSS treatment for 7 days led to substantial weight loss in both WT and Sesn2-/-/Sesn3-/- mice.
source: DSS treatment for 7 days led to substantial weight loss in both WT and Sesn2-/-/Sesn3-/- mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by body weight measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: WT mice recovered their body weight after being placed back on regular water following DSS treatment.
source: After placing back on regular water, WT mice recovered their body weight (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by body weight measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Sesn2-/-/Sesn3-/- mice did not show any recovery and continued to lose body weight until the experimental endpoint after DSS treatment.
source: However, Sesn2-/-/Sesn3-/- mice did not show any recovery and continued to lose body weight until the experimental endpoint (5 days during the recovery phase; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by body weight measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Sesn2-/-/Sesn3-/- mice showed a dramatic decrease in colon length when compared to WT mice after DSS treatment.
source: Sesn2-/-/Sesn3-/- mice also showed a dramatic decrease in colon length when compared to WT mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), indicative of strongly exacerbated DSS-induced colitis.
evidence: The claim is supported by colon length measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: WT mice exhibited substantial regeneration of epithelial structure at 5 days after DSS treatment.
source: Histological examination of colon tissue sections also revealed significant epithelial degeneration in Sesn2-/-/Sesn3-/- mice following the 5 days of recovery from the 7-day DSS treatment, while WT mice exhibited substantial regeneration of epithelial structure at the same time point (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by H&E staining shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Sesn2-/-/Sesn3-/- mice showed significant epithelial degeneration following 5 days of recovery from 7-day DSS treatment.
source: Histological examination of colon tissue sections also revealed significant epithelial degeneration in Sesn2-/-/Sesn3-/- mice following the 5 days of recovery from the 7-day DSS treatment, while WT mice exhibited substantial regeneration of epithelial structure at the same time point (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by H&E staining shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Both WT and Sesn2-/- mice develop severe colitis with one week of DSS treatment.
source: The increased susceptibility of Sesn2-/-/Sesn3-/- mice to DSS-induced injury (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C) was recapitulated in Sesn2-/- mice; although both WT and Sesn2-/- mice develop severe colitis with one week of DSS treatment (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2), WT mice successfully recovered from injury after one additional week of regular water treatment, while Sesn2-/- mice did not (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by body weight data in Figure 1D and histological data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: WT mice successfully recovered from DSS injury after one additional week of regular water treatment.
source: The increased susceptibility of Sesn2-/-/Sesn3-/- mice to DSS-induced injury (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C) was recapitulated in Sesn2-/- mice; although both WT and Sesn2-/- mice develop severe colitis with one week of DSS treatment (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2), WT mice successfully recovered from injury after one additional week of regular water treatment, while Sesn2-/- mice did not (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by body weight and histological data shown in Figure 1D-F.

claim: Sesn2-/- mice did not recover from DSS injury after one additional week of regular water treatment.
source: The increased susceptibility of Sesn2-/-/Sesn3-/- mice to DSS-induced injury (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C) was recapitulated in Sesn2-/- mice; although both WT and Sesn2-/- mice develop severe colitis with one week of DSS treatment (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2), WT mice successfully recovered from injury after one additional week of regular water treatment, while Sesn2-/- mice did not (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by body weight and histological data shown in Figure 1D-F.

claim: Sestrin2 has a critical role in restoring intestinal homeostasis after injury.
source: These results demonstrate a critical role for Sestrin2 in restoring intestinal homeostasis after injury.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that Sesn2-/- mice fail to recover from DSS-induced colitis (Figure 1D-F).

claim: WT mice displayed a very small number of apoptotic cells at 5 days after DSS injury.
source: At 5 days after DSS injury, WT mice displayed a very small number of apoptotic cells (Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), consistent with the histological observation showing that the colon epithelium had been restored (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by TUNEL staining shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: A significant number of apoptotic cells were observed in the colon epithelium of both Sesn2-/- and Sesn2-/-/Sesn3-/- mice at 5 days after DSS injury.
source: However, a significant number of apoptotic cells were observed in the colon epithelium of both Sesn2-/- and Sesn2-/-/Sesn3-/- mice (Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), consistent with the degenerative phenotypes observed in these mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by TUNEL staining shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: PCNA staining is confined to the base of colon crypts in WT mice after DSS recovery.
source: Proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA) staining of WT colon displayed a normal pattern of cell proliferation; PCNA staining is confined to the base of colon crypts in WT mice (Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), where epithelial progenitor cells are undergoing homeostatic proliferation that maintains normal turnover of the epithelium.
evidence: The claim is supported by PCNA immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The colon epithelium of both Sesn2-/- and Sesn2-/-/Sesn3-/- mice exhibited an increased number of PCNA-positive cells throughout the degenerated epithelium.
source: However, the colon epithelium of both Sesn2-/- and Sesn2-/-/Sesn3-/- mice exhibited an increased number of PCNA-positive cells throughout the degenerated epithelium (Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by PCNA immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Colonocytes of both Sesn2-/- and Sesn2-/-/Sesn3-/- mice were undergoing active proliferation to compensate for the apoptotic loss of epithelial cells.
source: This result suggests that, in order to compensate for the apoptotic loss of epithelial cells, colonocytes of both Sesn2-/- and Sesn2-/-/Sesn3-/- mice were undergoing active proliferation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the increased PCNA staining throughout the degenerated epithelium in Sesn2-/- and Sesn2-/-/Sesn3-/- mice (Figure 1H).

claim: Sesn2-/- mice had increased levels of colon inflammation after DSS injury.
source: Immunohistochemical staining of macrophage marker F4/80 (Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F), as well as quantitative RT-PCR examination of inflammation markers Tnfa (Figure 1J), Il6 (Figure 1K), Il1b (Figure 1L) and Il10 (Figure 1M), show that Sesn2-/- mice had increased the levels of colon inflammation after DSS injury.
evidence: The claim is supported by F4/80 immunohistochemistry (Figure 1I) and qRT-PCR data for inflammation markers (Figure 1J-M).

claim: Sestrin2 deficiency exacerbates DSS-induced colon damage and inflammation.
source: These data collectively indicate that Sestrin2 deficiency exacerbates DSS-induced colon damage and inflammation.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple lines of evidence including increased apoptosis, proliferation, and inflammation markers in Sesn2-/- mice after DSS treatment (Figure 1G-M).

claim: Inflammatory cytokine signaling instigated by bone marrow-derived immune cells is important for the progression of colitis.
source: Inflammatory cytokine signaling instigated by bone marrow-derived immune cells, such as macrophages, is known to be important for the progression of colitis as well as colon cancer (Terzic et al, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Terzic et al, 2010.

claim: Inflammatory cytokine signaling instigated by bone marrow-derived immune cells is important for the progression of colon cancer.
source: Inflammatory cytokine signaling instigated by bone marrow-derived immune cells, such as macrophages, is known to be important for the progression of colitis as well as colon cancer (Terzic et al, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Terzic et al, 2010.

claim: Sn2→WT mice were able to recover from DSS-induced injury.
source: Interestingly, Sn2→WT mice were similar to WT mice and able to recover from DSS-induced injury (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by body weight and survival data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: More than 70% of WT→Sn2 mice were dead at 6 days following DSS treatment.
source: However, more than 70% of WT→Sn2 mice were dead at 6 days following DSS treatment (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: WT→Sn2 mice experienced dramatic weight loss during the recovery phase following DSS treatment.
source: WT→Sn2 mice, but not Sn2→WT mice, also experienced dramatic weight loss during the recovery phase following DSS treatment (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by body weight data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The epithelial structure of Sn2→WT mouse colon was nearly completely restored at 6 days after DSS treatment.
source: Histological examination of the surviving mice revealed that, although the epithelial structure of Sn2→WT mouse colon was nearly completely restored at 6 days after the DSS treatment, WT→Sn2 colon epithelium was degenerated and marked by complete loss of epithelial cells and a robust increase in infiltrating immune cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by H&E staining shown in Figure 2C.

claim: WT→Sn2 colon epithelium was degenerated and marked by complete loss of epithelial cells and a robust increase in infiltrating immune cells at 6 days after DSS treatment.
source: Histological examination of the surviving mice revealed that, although the epithelial structure of Sn2→WT mouse colon was nearly completely restored at 6 days after the DSS treatment, WT→Sn2 colon epithelium was degenerated and marked by complete loss of epithelial cells and a robust increase in infiltrating immune cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by H&E staining shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The hematopoietic compartment of recipient mice had been completely substituted with bone marrow cells of the donor in bone marrow chimera experiments.
source: Genotyping of spleen tissues in surviving WT→Sn2 and Sn2→WT mice confirmed that the hematopoietic compartment of recipient mice had been completely substituted with bone marrow cells of the donor (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by genotyping data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The extra-hematopoietic presence of Sestrin2 is critical for the maintenance of intestinal homeostasis during colitis.
source: These results indicate that the extra-hematopoietic presence of Sestrin2, such as in epithelial cells, is critical for the maintenance of intestinal homeostasis during colitis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from bone marrow chimera experiments showing that WT→Sn2 mice (lacking Sestrin2 in non-hematopoietic cells) fail to recover from DSS injury while Sn2→WT mice (having Sestrin2 in non-hematopoietic cells) recover successfully (Figure 2A-C).

claim: Sestrin2 protects cells and tissues from ER stress and its pathological sequelae such as metabolic abnormalities, tissue inflammation and apoptotic cell death.
source: Sestrin2 protects cells and tissues from ER stress and its pathological sequelae such as metabolic abnormalities, tissue inflammation and apoptotic cell death (Park et al, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Park et al, 2014.

claim: DSS treatment can induce ER stress in colon epithelia.
source: DSS treatment was recently found to induce ER stress in colon epithelia (Cao et al, 2013), and consistent with this report, we observed that DSS treatment can induce prolonged ER stress signaling that is associated with modestly elevated Sestrin2 expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Cao et al, 2013 and by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: DSS treatment can induce prolonged ER stress signaling that is associated with modestly elevated Sestrin2 expression.
source: DSS treatment was recently found to induce ER stress in colon epithelia (Cao et al, 2013), and consistent with this report, we observed that DSS treatment can induce prolonged ER stress signaling that is associated with modestly elevated Sestrin2 expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing increased ER stress markers and Sestrin2 expression after DSS treatment in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Sesn2-/- and Sesn2-/-/Sesn3-/- mice have elevated phosphorylation of PERK compared to WT mice after DSS injury.
source: Immunoblot analyses of colon tissue showed that Sesn2-/- and Sesn2-/-/Sesn3-/- mice have elevated phosphorylation of pancreatic ER kinase (PERK) and increased expression of BiP and CHOP (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B), when compared to WT mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: Sesn2-/- and Sesn2-/-/Sesn3-/- mice have increased expression of BiP compared to WT mice after DSS injury.
source: Immunoblot analyses of colon tissue showed that Sesn2-/- and Sesn2-/-/Sesn3-/- mice have elevated phosphorylation of pancreatic ER kinase (PERK) and increased expression of BiP and CHOP (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B), when compared to WT mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: Sesn2-/- and Sesn2-/-/Sesn3-/- mice have increased expression of CHOP compared to WT mice after DSS injury.
source: Immunoblot analyses of colon tissue showed that Sesn2-/- and Sesn2-/-/Sesn3-/- mice have elevated phosphorylation of pancreatic ER kinase (PERK) and increased expression of BiP and CHOP (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B), when compared to WT mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: mRNA expression of spliced XBP1 (XBP1s) was robustly upregulated in the colon of Sesn2-/- mice after DSS injury.
source: mRNA expression analysis for ER stress target genes, including spliced XBP1 (XBP1s) and BiP cofactor ERdj4, were also robustly upregulated in the colon of Sesn2-/- mice (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: mRNA expression of BiP cofactor ERdj4 was robustly upregulated in the colon of Sesn2-/- mice after DSS injury.
source: mRNA expression analysis for ER stress target genes, including spliced XBP1 (XBP1s) and BiP cofactor ERdj4, were also robustly upregulated in the colon of Sesn2-/- mice (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Immunostaining confirmed the presence of prominent ER stress in the damaged colon epithelium of Sesn2-/- mice.
source: Immunostaining of BiP and CHOP also confirmed the presence of prominent ER stress in the damaged colon epithelium of Sesn2-/- mice (Figure 2G,H and Figure 2—figure supplement 2D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data for BiP and CHOP shown in Figure 2G,H and Figure 2—figure supplement 2D,E.

claim: Endogenous Sestrin2 is critical for the suppression of colon ER stress after DSS insults.
source: These results collectively indicate that endogenous Sestrin2 is critical for the suppression of colon ER stress after DSS insults.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple lines of evidence showing elevated ER stress markers in Sesn2-/- mice after DSS treatment (Figure 2E-H).

claim: Pre-existing colitis is important for the progression of colon cancer.
source: Since pre-existing colitis (Terzic et al, 2010) or tumor-elicited inflammation (Grivennikov et al, 2012) is important for the progression of colon cancer, it is possible that Sestrin2 expression is lost or downregulated during colon carcinogenesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Terzic et al, 2010.

claim: Tumor-elicited inflammation is important for the progression of colon cancer.
source: Since pre-existing colitis (Terzic et al, 2010) or tumor-elicited inflammation (Grivennikov et al, 2012) is important for the progression of colon cancer, it is possible that Sestrin2 expression is lost or downregulated during colon carcinogenesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Grivennikov et al, 2012.

claim: Human Sestrin2 (SESN2) mRNA expression was strongly downregulated in colon adenocarcinoma tissues when compared to normal colon controls in virtually all colon cancer transcriptome studies in the Oncomine database.
source: Surprisingly, in virtually all of the colon cancer transcriptome studies available within the database, which were conducted in diverse platforms using different patient tissues, human Sestrin2 (SESN2) mRNA expression was strongly downregulated in colon adenocarcinoma tissues when compared to normal colon controls (Figure 3A–G) (Gaspar et al, 2008; Graudens et al, 2006; Hong et al, 2010; Kaiser et al, 2007; Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2012; Skrzypczak et al, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by data mining of multiple independent studies shown in Figure 3A-G and cited references.

claim: The magnitude of SESN2 suppression in tumors is often among the top 1–5% of all suppressed genes.
source: The magnitude of SESN2 suppression in tumors is often among the top 1–5% of all suppressed genes (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Oncomine analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The downregulation of SESN2 mRNA in colon cancer is specific and not an indirect consequence of different compositions of cell subtypes between normal and tumor tissues.
source: In contrast, other major cell type markers, such as Villin (VIL1, enterocytes), DLL1 (progenitor cells), F4/80 (EMR1, macrophages), Gr-1 (LY6G5B, leukocytes), or β-catenin (CTNNB, colon epithelia), did not show such strong suppression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–E), while the stem cell marker LGR5 was rather upregulated in tumor samples (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–E). These results indicate that the downregulation of SESN2 mRNA in colon cancer is specific and not an indirect consequence of different compositions of cell subtypes between normal and tumor tissues.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparison of SESN2 expression changes with other cell type markers shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-E.

claim: SESN2 genome copy is significantly reduced in colon cancer.
source: SESN2 genome copy is also significantly reduced in colon cancer, and decreases further as the colon cancer progresses (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA copy number analysis from TCGA dataset shown in Figure 3H.

claim: SESN2 genome copy decreases further as colon cancer progresses.
source: SESN2 genome copy is also significantly reduced in colon cancer, and decreases further as the colon cancer progresses (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA copy number analysis from TCGA dataset shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Transcriptional downregulation, rather than the loss of genomic information, is the major mechanism of SESN2 inhibition during colon cancer progression.
source: However, the extent of copy number loss was very small (~10%), suggesting that transcriptional downregulation, rather than the loss of genomic information, is the major mechanism of SESN2 inhibition during colon cancer progression.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that SESN2 copy number loss is only ~10% while mRNA expression is much more dramatically reduced (Figure 3).

claim: SESN2 is a transcriptional target of tumor suppressor p53.
source: SESN2 is a transcriptional target of tumor suppressor p53 (Budanov et al, 2002), which is one of the most frequently mutated genes in colon cancer (Fearon, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Budanov et al, 2002.

claim: p53 is one of the most frequently mutated genes in colon cancer.
source: SESN2 is a transcriptional target of tumor suppressor p53 (Budanov et al, 2002), which is one of the most frequently mutated genes in colon cancer (Fearon, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Fearon, 2011.

claim: SESN2 expression is significantly reduced in 'p53-mutated' tumors when compared to 'p53-unknown' tumors.
source: The analyses demonstrated that SESN2 expression is significantly reduced in 'p53-mutated' tumors when compared to 'p53-unknown' tumors (Figure 4A), suggesting a role of p53 in controlling SESN2 expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of TCGA dataset partitioned by p53 status shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There were almost no overlaps of SESN2 expression levels between the normal colon and 'p53-mutated' tumor groups.
source: Strikingly, there were almost no overlaps of SESN2 expression levels between the normal colon and 'p53-mutated' tumor groups (Figure 4B,C), while SESN2 levels in 'p53-unknown' tumors overlap with both groups (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by scatter plot analysis shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: SESN2 levels in 'p53-unknown' tumors overlap with both normal colon and 'p53-mutated' tumor groups.
source: Strikingly, there were almost no overlaps of SESN2 expression levels between the normal colon and 'p53-mutated' tumor groups (Figure 4B,C), while SESN2 levels in 'p53-unknown' tumors overlap with both groups (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by scatter plot analysis shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: Expression levels of CDKN1A, GADD45A, and MDM2 have a general positive correlation with expression of SESN2 in individual samples.
source: Nevertheless, expression levels of these genes have a general positive correlation with expression of SESN2 in individual samples (Figure 4D–F), suggesting that SESN2, CDKN1A, GADD45A and MDM2 are all regulated through the same p53-dependent mechanism.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4D-F.

claim: SESN2, CDKN1A, GADD45A and MDM2 are all regulated through the same p53-dependent mechanism.
source: Nevertheless, expression levels of these genes have a general positive correlation with expression of SESN2 in individual samples (Figure 4D–F), suggesting that SESN2, CDKN1A, GADD45A and MDM2 are all regulated through the same p53-dependent mechanism.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the positive correlation between these genes and their differential expression between p53-mutated and p53-unknown tumors (Figure 4).

claim: SESN2 is a clinically relevant target of p53 during colon carcinogenesis.
source: These results collectively highlight SESN2 as a clinically relevant target of p53 during colon carcinogenesis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the strong correlation between p53 status and SESN2 expression in human colon cancer samples (Figure 4).

claim: Two-year-old WT and Sesn2-/- mice did not reveal any noticeable colon tumors.
source: The analysis of two-year-old WT and Sesn2-/- mice (n=6 each) did not reveal any noticeable colon tumors, suggesting that Sesn2 may not be a classical tumor suppressor gene whose homozygous deletion is sufficient to induce spontaneous cancer development.
evidence: The claim is supported by observation of aged mice.

claim: Sesn2 may not be a classical tumor suppressor gene whose homozygous deletion is sufficient to induce spontaneous cancer development.
source: The analysis of two-year-old WT and Sesn2-/- mice (n=6 each) did not reveal any noticeable colon tumors, suggesting that Sesn2 may not be a classical tumor suppressor gene whose homozygous deletion is sufficient to induce spontaneous cancer development.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of spontaneous tumors in aged Sesn2-/- mice.

claim: None of Sesn2-/- mice survived the first round of colitis induction in the standard AOM-DSS protocol.
source: However, none of Sesn2-/- mice (n=7) survived the first round of colitis induction (Figure 5A), while WT mice were able to survive the entirety of the treatment.
evidence: The claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: WT mice were able to survive the entirety of the standard AOM-DSS treatment.
source: However, none of Sesn2-/- mice (n=7) survived the first round of colitis induction (Figure 5A), while WT mice were able to survive the entirety of the treatment.
evidence: The claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Sestrin2 has an important physiological role in maintaining epithelial integrity during colon injury.
source: This is consistent with our findings that Sestrin2 has an important physiological role in maintaining epithelial integrity during colon injury (Figures 1–2).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the DSS colitis experiments showing that Sesn2-/- mice fail to recover from colon injury (Figures 1-2).

claim: Tumor size and burden were dramatically increased in Sesn2-/- mice in the modified AOM-DSS model.
source: However, tumor size (Figure 5E,F) and burden (Figure 5G) were dramatically increased in Sesn2-/- mice, suggesting that Sestrin2 loss promoted tumor growth and progression in the colitis-associated cancer model.
evidence: The claim is supported by tumor size and burden measurements shown in Figure 5E-G.

claim: Sestrin2 loss promoted tumor growth and progression in the colitis-associated cancer model.
source: However, tumor size (Figure 5E,F) and burden (Figure 5G) were dramatically increased in Sesn2-/- mice, suggesting that Sestrin2 loss promoted tumor growth and progression in the colitis-associated cancer model.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the increased tumor size and burden in Sesn2-/- mice (Figure 5E-G).

claim: Tumors developed in both WT and Sesn2-/- mice displayed classical characteristics of colon adenomas.
source: Tumors developed in both WT and Sesn2-/- mice displayed classical characteristics of colon adenomas, such as nuclear β-catenin staining (Figure 5H), increased cell proliferation (Figure 5I; PCNA staining), DNA damage (Figure 5J; γ-H2AX staining) and apoptotic cell death (Figure 5K; TUNEL staining).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry and TUNEL staining shown in Figure 5H-K.

claim: Tumor cell proliferation is significantly increased in tumors isolated from Sesn2-/- mice.
source: Quantification of PCNA-, γ-H2AX- and TUNEL-positive cells showed that tumor cell proliferation (Figure 5L) is significantly increased in tumors isolated from Sesn2-/- mice, while DNA damage (Figure 5M) and apoptosis (Figure 5N) were not significantly altered by the loss of Sestrin2.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of PCNA-positive cells shown in Figure 5L.

claim: DNA damage was not significantly altered by the loss of Sestrin2 in colon tumors.
source: Quantification of PCNA-, γ-H2AX- and TUNEL-positive cells showed that tumor cell proliferation (Figure 5L) is significantly increased in tumors isolated from Sesn2-/- mice, while DNA damage (Figure 5M) and apoptosis (Figure 5N) were not significantly altered by the loss of Sestrin2.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of γ-H2AX-positive cells shown in Figure 5M.

claim: Apoptosis was not significantly altered by the loss of Sestrin2 in colon tumors.
source: Quantification of PCNA-, γ-H2AX- and TUNEL-positive cells showed that tumor cell proliferation (Figure 5L) is significantly increased in tumors isolated from Sesn2-/- mice, while DNA damage (Figure 5M) and apoptosis (Figure 5N) were not significantly altered by the loss of Sestrin2.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of TUNEL-positive cells shown in Figure 5N.

claim: WT→Sn2 mice exhibited strongly exacerbated tumor growth phenotypes compared to Sn2→WT mice.
source: Compared to the Sn2→WT mice, WT→Sn2 mice exhibited strongly exacerbated tumor growth phenotypes, which was evident in both tumor number and size (Figure 6A–D), indicating that the extra-hematopoietic expression of Sestrin2, such as in colon epithelia, is critical for colon tumor suppression.
evidence: The claim is supported by tumor analysis in bone marrow chimera mice shown in Figure 6A-D.

claim: The extra-hematopoietic expression of Sestrin2 is critical for colon tumor suppression.
source: Compared to the Sn2→WT mice, WT→Sn2 mice exhibited strongly exacerbated tumor growth phenotypes, which was evident in both tumor number and size (Figure 6A–D), indicating that the extra-hematopoietic expression of Sestrin2, such as in colon epithelia, is critical for colon tumor suppression.
evidence: The claim is inferred from bone marrow chimera experiments showing that WT→Sn2 mice (lacking Sestrin2 in non-hematopoietic cells) develop more tumors than Sn2→WT mice (Figure 6A-D).

claim: Phosphorylation of ribosomal protein S6 is dramatically increased in tumors isolated from Sesn2-/- mice.
source: Phosphorylation of ribosomal protein S6, which is mediated by an mTORC1 target p70 S6 kinase (S6K), is dramatically increased in tumors isolated from Sesn2-/- mice (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Phosphorylation of 4E-BP was prominently increased in Sesn2-/- colon cancer tissues compared to adjacent normal colon tissues and to WT colon cancer tissues.
source: Consistent with this observation, phosphorylation of eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4E-binding protein (4E-BP), an additional mTORC1 target, was also prominently increased in Sesn2-/- colon cancer tissues, when compared to adjacent normal colon tissues as well as to WT colon cancer tissues (Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: S6 and 4E-BP phosphorylation was prominently increased in colon tumors of Sesn2-/- mice compared to those of WT mice.
source: These immunohistochemical observations were also confirmed by immunoblotting experiments; S6 and 4E-BP phosphorylation was prominently increased in colon tumors of Sesn2-/- mice, compared to those of WT mice (Figure 6G–I and Figure 6—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6G-I and Figure 6—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Tumors from WT→Sn2 mice exhibited hyperactive mTORC1 signaling indicated by increased S6 phosphorylation.
source: Tumors from WT→Sn2 mice, but not those from Sn2→WT mice, also exhibited hyperactive mTORC1 signaling, indicated by increased S6 phosphorylation (Figure 6J–L and Figure 6—figure supplement 2C,3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry and immunoblot data shown in Figure 6J-L and Figure 6—figure supplement 2C,3B.

claim: AKT Ser473 phosphorylation was not significantly altered by Sestrin2 loss in colon cancer tissues.
source: However, AKT Ser473 phosphorylation, which is mediated by mTORC2, a complex distinct from mTORC1, was not significantly altered by Sestrin2 loss in colon cancer tissues (Figure 6G).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Sestrin2 loss selectively leads to mTORC1 hyperactivation in colon cancer tissues.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that Sestrin2 loss selectively leads to mTORC1 hyperactivation in colon cancer tissues, which subsequently allowed for prominent tumor overgrowth.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that mTORC1 substrates (S6, 4E-BP) but not mTORC2 substrate (AKT) are hyperphosphorylated in Sesn2-/- tumors (Figure 6).

claim: mTORC1 hyperactivation due to Sestrin2 loss allowed for prominent tumor overgrowth.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that Sestrin2 loss selectively leads to mTORC1 hyperactivation in colon cancer tissues, which subsequently allowed for prominent tumor overgrowth.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the correlation between mTORC1 hyperactivation and increased tumor size in Sesn2-/- mice (Figures 5-6).

claim: Mouse colon cancers induced by AOM-DSS treatment displayed Sestrin2 expression at a level comparable to that of normal colon tissues.
source: Unlike human colon cancer tissues (Figures 3,4), mouse colon cancers induced by the AOM-DSS treatment displayed Sestrin2 expression at a level comparable to that of normal colon tissues (Figure 6G).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Most mouse colon tumors induced by AOM-DSS treatment do not contain p53 mutations or misregulation.
source: Interestingly, it has been formerly reported that most mouse colon tumors induced by the AOM-DSS treatment do not contain p53 mutations or misregulation (Nambiar et al, 2004; Takahashi and Wakabayashi, 2004), and this may provide an explanation of why Sestrin2 expression is sustained in this specific mouse model of colon cancer.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Nambiar et al, 2004; Takahashi and Wakabayashi, 2004.

claim: SW480 cells demonstrated a strong downregulation of Sestrin2 expression.
source: Indeed, SW480 cells, a human colon cancer cell line that displays very low p53 activity, demonstrated a strong downregulation of Sestrin2 expression, while RKO and HCT116 cells, which have wild-type p53 activity, expressed a relatively high amount of Sestrin2 proteins (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: RKO and HCT116 cells expressed a relatively high amount of Sestrin2 proteins.
source: Indeed, SW480 cells, a human colon cancer cell line that displays very low p53 activity, demonstrated a strong downregulation of Sestrin2 expression, while RKO and HCT116 cells, which have wild-type p53 activity, expressed a relatively high amount of Sestrin2 proteins (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: p53-deficient HCT116 cells exhibited dramatic downregulation of Sestrin2 expression when compared to the parental HCT116 cells.
source: The p53-deficient HCT116 cells exhibited dramatic downregulation of Sestrin2 expression when compared to the parental HCT116 cells (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Expression of Sestrin2 in hyperplastic mouse colon tissues was reduced by the loss of p53 or a dominant-negative mutation of p53.
source: Expression of Sestrin2 in hyperplastic mouse colon tissues, which have mutations in both Apc and Kras genes (Feng et al, 2013), was also reduced by the loss of p53 or a dominant-negative mutation of p53 (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data from genetically modified mouse colon tissues shown in Figure 7C.

claim: p53 is critical for Sestrin2 expression in colon cancer cells.
source: Consistent with clinical data on human SESN2 expression described above (Figure 4), these results further support the notion that p53 is critical for Sestrin2 expression in colon cancer cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple lines of evidence showing correlation between p53 status and Sestrin2 expression in cell lines and mouse models (Figure 7A-C).

claim: Restoration of Sestrin2 suppressed serum-induced phosphorylation of mTORC1 substrates S6K and 4E-BP in p53-deficient HCT116 cells and SW480 cells.
source: Restoration of Sestrin2 suppressed serum-induced phosphorylation of mTORC1 substrates, S6K and 4E-BP (Figure 7D,E), but not mTORC2 substrate AKT (Figure 7E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 7D,E.

claim: Restoration of Sestrin2 did not suppress serum-induced phosphorylation of mTORC2 substrate AKT.
source: Restoration of Sestrin2 suppressed serum-induced phosphorylation of mTORC1 substrates, S6K and 4E-BP (Figure 7D,E), but not mTORC2 substrate AKT (Figure 7E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Sestrin2 silencing in RKO cells enhanced mTORC1 signaling in both starved and serum-stimulated cells.
source: Sestrin2 silencing in RKO cells enhanced the mTORC1 signaling in both starved and serum-stimulated cells (Figure 7F), indicating that endogenous Sestrin2 indeed functions to inhibit mTORC1 signaling in human colon cancer cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Endogenous Sestrin2 functions to inhibit mTORC1 signaling in human colon cancer cells.
source: Sestrin2 silencing in RKO cells enhanced the mTORC1 signaling in both starved and serum-stimulated cells (Figure 7F), indicating that endogenous Sestrin2 indeed functions to inhibit mTORC1 signaling in human colon cancer cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Sestrin2 silencing enhances mTORC1 signaling (Figure 7F).

claim: Sestrin2-silenced RKO cells demonstrated an increase in clonogenic growth compared to control cells.
source: A colony forming assay of Sestrin2-silenced RKO cells demonstrated an increase in clonogenic growth compared to the control cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B), suggesting that Sestrin2 is an inhibitor of cancer cell growth.
evidence: The claim is supported by colony forming assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Sestrin2 is an inhibitor of cancer cell growth.
source: A colony forming assay of Sestrin2-silenced RKO cells demonstrated an increase in clonogenic growth compared to the control cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B), suggesting that Sestrin2 is an inhibitor of cancer cell growth.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the increased clonogenic growth in Sestrin2-silenced cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B).

claim: Rapamycin inhibited clonogenic growth in both control and Sestrin2-silenced cells.
source: Rapamycin inhibited clonogenic growth in both control and Sestrin2-silenced cells, and interestingly, the growth difference between control and Sestrin2-silenced cells was diminished upon rapamycin treatment (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by colony forming assay data with rapamycin treatment shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The growth difference between control and Sestrin2-silenced cells was diminished upon rapamycin treatment.
source: Rapamycin inhibited clonogenic growth in both control and Sestrin2-silenced cells, and interestingly, the growth difference between control and Sestrin2-silenced cells was diminished upon rapamycin treatment (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by colony forming assay data with rapamycin treatment shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Sestrin2 attenuates cancer cell growth primarily through inhibition of hyperactive mTORC1.
source: These results indicate that Sestrin2 attenuates cancer cell growth primarily through inhibition of a hyperactive mTORC1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that rapamycin treatment eliminates the growth difference between control and Sestrin2-silenced cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B).

claim: Expression of Sestrin2 in SW480 cells substantially inhibited clonogenic growth.
source: On the other hand, expression of Sestrin2 in SW480 cells substantially inhibited clonogenic growth (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C,D), supporting the idea that Sestrin2 is critical for inhibition of colon cancer cell overgrowth.
evidence: The claim is supported by colony forming assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Sestrin2 is critical for inhibition of colon cancer cell overgrowth.
source: On the other hand, expression of Sestrin2 in SW480 cells substantially inhibited clonogenic growth (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C,D), supporting the idea that Sestrin2 is critical for inhibition of colon cancer cell overgrowth.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Sestrin2 expression inhibits clonogenic growth in SW480 cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C,D).

claim: Sestrin2 silencing rendered RKO cells less susceptible to 5-FU and CPT-11 treatments.
source: Although control cell growth was strongly suppressed by 5-FU or CPT-11, Sestrin2 silencing rendered cells less susceptible to the chemotherapeutic drug treatments (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–C), suggesting that Sestrin2 loss may confer chemotherapy resistance to colon cancer cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by colony forming assay data with chemotherapy treatment shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A-C.

claim: Sestrin2 loss may confer chemotherapy resistance to colon cancer cells.
source: Although control cell growth was strongly suppressed by 5-FU or CPT-11, Sestrin2 silencing rendered cells less susceptible to the chemotherapeutic drug treatments (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–C), suggesting that Sestrin2 loss may confer chemotherapy resistance to colon cancer cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the reduced susceptibility to chemotherapy in Sestrin2-silenced cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A-C).

claim: Sestrin2 expression was slightly elevated in RKO cells after 5-FU or CPT-11 treatments.
source: After 5-FU or CPT-11 treatments, Sestrin2 expression was slightly elevated in WT cells (sh-Luc; Figure 7—figure supplement 2D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2D,E.

claim: mTORC1 signaling was prominently upregulated in sh-SESN2 cells after 5-FU treatment.
source: Interestingly, mTORC1 signaling, monitored by p-S6K and p-4E-BP1, was prominently upregulated in sh-SESN2 cells after 5-FU treatment (Figure 7—figure supplement 2D), suggesting that Sestrin2 suppresses mTORC1 activation after 5-FU treatment.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Sestrin2 suppresses mTORC1 activation after 5-FU treatment.
source: Interestingly, mTORC1 signaling, monitored by p-S6K and p-4E-BP1, was prominently upregulated in sh-SESN2 cells after 5-FU treatment (Figure 7—figure supplement 2D), suggesting that Sestrin2 suppresses mTORC1 activation after 5-FU treatment.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that mTORC1 signaling is upregulated in Sestrin2-silenced cells after 5-FU treatment (Figure 7—figure supplement 2D).

claim: CPT-11 treatment reduced mTORC1 signaling in RKO cells.
source: In contrast, CPT-11 treatment reduced mTORC1 signaling, and Sestrin2 silencing led to modest but persistent mTORC1 upregulation (Figure 7—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Sestrin2 silencing led to modest but persistent mTORC1 upregulation after CPT-11 treatment.
source: In contrast, CPT-11 treatment reduced mTORC1 signaling, and Sestrin2 silencing led to modest but persistent mTORC1 upregulation (Figure 7—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2E.

claim: mTORC1 upregulation as a result of Sestrin2 loss could have conferred chemoresistance to RKO cells against 5-FU and CPT-11.
source: This mTORC1 upregulation as a result of Sestrin2 loss could have conferred chemoresistance to RKO cells against 5-FU and CPT-11.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the correlation between mTORC1 upregulation and chemoresistance in Sestrin2-silenced cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).

claim: During colitis stress, Sestrin2 functions to suppress ER stress and to promote regeneration of colon epithelium.
source: During colitis stress, Sestrin2 functions to suppress ER stress and to promote regeneration of colon epithelium (Figures 1,2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that Sesn2-/- mice have elevated ER stress and impaired epithelial regeneration after DSS treatment (Figures 1-2).

claim: Expression of Sestrin2 is important for suppressing hyperactive mTORC1 signaling in colon cancer.
source: Because expression of Sestrin2 is important for suppressing hyperactive mTORC1 signaling (Figure 6) and tumor outgrowth (Figure 5), loss of Sestrin2 expression in human colon cancer serves as a critical tumorigenic mechanism.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing hyperactive mTORC1 signaling in Sesn2-/- tumors (Figure 6).

claim: Expression of Sestrin2 is important for suppressing tumor outgrowth.
source: Because expression of Sestrin2 is important for suppressing hyperactive mTORC1 signaling (Figure 6) and tumor outgrowth (Figure 5), loss of Sestrin2 expression in human colon cancer serves as a critical tumorigenic mechanism.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing increased tumor size in Sesn2-/- mice (Figure 5).

claim: Loss of Sestrin2 expression in human colon cancer serves as a critical tumorigenic mechanism.
source: Because expression of Sestrin2 is important for suppressing hyperactive mTORC1 signaling (Figure 6) and tumor outgrowth (Figure 5), loss of Sestrin2 expression in human colon cancer serves as a critical tumorigenic mechanism.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combination of human data showing SESN2 downregulation in colon cancer (Figure 3) and mouse data showing tumor promotion by Sestrin2 loss (Figures 5-6).

claim: Sestrin2 negatively controlled cell growth in various human colon cancer cell lines, which was dependent on mTORC1 regulation.
source: Indeed, Sestrin2 negatively controlled cell growth in various human colon cancer cell lines, which was dependent on mTORC1 regulation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by colony forming assay data showing that Sestrin2 inhibits cell growth and that this effect is abolished by rapamycin (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).

claim: Inactivation of Sestrin2 conferred chemoresistance to colon cancer cells.
source: Furthermore, inactivation of Sestrin2 conferred chemoresistance to colon cancer cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 2), rendering them difficult to treat with conventional chemotherapeutic methods.
evidence: The claim is supported by colony forming assay data showing reduced susceptibility to 5-FU and CPT-11 in Sestrin2-silenced cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).

claim: Sestrin2 is known to reduce oxidative stress by functioning as an activator of anti-ROS transcription factor Nrf2.
source: In addition to mTORC1 regulation, Sestrin2 is also known to reduce oxidative stress (Budanov et al, 2004) by functioning as an activator of anti-ROS transcription factor Nrf2 (Bae et al, 2013) or as an alkylhydroperoxidase (Kim et al, 2015a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Budanov et al, 2004 and Bae et al, 2013.

claim: Sestrin2 is known to reduce oxidative stress by functioning as an alkylhydroperoxidase.
source: In addition to mTORC1 regulation, Sestrin2 is also known to reduce oxidative stress (Budanov et al, 2004) by functioning as an activator of anti-ROS transcription factor Nrf2 (Bae et al, 2013) or as an alkylhydroperoxidase (Kim et al, 2015a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Budanov et al, 2004 and Kim et al, 2015a.

claim: The mTORC1-regulatory function, rather than the ROS-inhibiting function, is the main contributor of Sestrin2's tumor suppressive activity in colon tissues.
source: This result suggests that the mTORC1-regulatory function, rather than the ROS-inhibiting function, is the main contributor of Sestrin2's tumor suppressive activity in colon tissues.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that DNA damage (γ-H2AX) was not significantly increased in Sesn2-/- tumors (Figure 5J,M), suggesting ROS is not the primary mechanism.

claim: Sestrin2 may attenuate tumor growth, at least partially by inhibiting tumor-associated epithelial damage and inflammation.
source: Nevertheless, it is still possible that Sestrin2 attenuates tumor growth, at least partially by inhibiting tumor-associated epithelial damage and inflammation (Figures 1,2), which are well-characterized promoters of colon cancer growth (Grivennikov et al, 2012; Terzic et al, 2010).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the observation that Sestrin2 protects against colitis (Figures 1-2) and citations showing inflammation promotes cancer.

claim: Sestrin2 may exert tumor suppressive activity through its apoptosis-inducing function.
source: It is also possible that Sestrin2 exerts tumor suppressive activity additionally through its apoptosis-inducing function, which was recently discovered (Ding et al, 2015).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on citation to Ding et al, 2015.

claim: The mTORC1-suppressing and ROS-reducing activities are shared between all members of the Sestrin family (Sestrin1-3).
source: The mTORC1-suppressing and ROS-reducing activities are shared between all members of the Sestrin family (Sestrin1-3) (Lee et al, 2013; Nogueira et al, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lee et al, 2013; Nogueira et al, 2008.

claim: Only Sestrin2 was shown to be downregulated in human colon cancer tissues.
source: However, only Sestrin2 was shown to be downregulated in human colon cancer tissues, and expression of Sestrin1 and Sestrin3 was unchanged or slightly upregulated in the colon cancer tissues.
evidence: The claim is supported by Oncomine analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Expression of Sestrin1 and Sestrin3 was unchanged or slightly upregulated in colon cancer tissues.
source: However, only Sestrin2 was shown to be downregulated in human colon cancer tissues, and expression of Sestrin1 and Sestrin3 was unchanged or slightly upregulated in the colon cancer tissues.
evidence: The claim is supported by Oncomine analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Sestrin1 and Sestrin3 are strongly downregulated in several types of cancer tissues, such as lung cancers and lymphomas.
source: Nevertheless, Sestrin1 and Sestrin3 are strongly downregulated in several types of cancer tissues, such as lung cancers and lymphomas (Figure 3A), suggesting that they may be involved in anti-tumorigenic processes in tissues other than the colon.
evidence: The claim is supported by Oncomine analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Sestrin1 and Sestrin3 may be involved in anti-tumorigenic processes in tissues other than the colon.
source: Nevertheless, Sestrin1 and Sestrin3 are strongly downregulated in several types of cancer tissues, such as lung cancers and lymphomas (Figure 3A), suggesting that they may be involved in anti-tumorigenic processes in tissues other than the colon.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the downregulation of Sestrin1 and Sestrin3 in other cancer types (Figure 3A).

claim: Drosophila Sestrin was shown to be a feedback inhibitor of mTORC1, which can suppress hyperplastic tissue growth provoked by oncogenic mTORC1 hyperactivation.
source: Drosophila Sestrin, which is the only Sestrin homologue expressed in Drosophila, was formerly shown to be a feedback inhibitor of mTORC1, which can suppress hyperplastic tissue growth provoked by oncogenic mTORC1 hyperactivation (Lee et al, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lee et al, 2010.
